response: {"title":"Import-closure verification","intervention":"Run tests covering changed modules and their reverse-import closure in increasing historical or observed runtime order, stopping after the first failure for diagnosis and reserving enough time to rerun that failing check once after repair.","claim":"Relative to no appended instruction, this import-closure ordering will improve hidden-test pass_rate without increasing deadline misses on deadline-bound multi-module Python tasks.","mechanism":"Reverse imports approximate the regression blast radius, shortest-first ordering accumulates coverage quickly, and a protected rerun budget converts detected failures into verified repairs instead of late unconfirmed edits.","assumptions":["Python import relationships approximate behavioral dependency for the benchmark.","Test runtimes are available or can be estimated from test scope.","Most first failures are sufficiently diagnostic to justify pausing the remaining suite."],"risks":["Dynamic imports and data dependencies may be absent from the import closure.","Shortest-first can delay a uniquely valuable slow test.","Stopping at the first failure can hide independent defects.","Reserved rerun time may go unused on passing tasks."],"test_plan":{"experiment":"Randomize matched multi-module Python tasks to treatment or no-instruction control with the same deadline, model, tools, and hidden tests; log completion and verification commands.","metrics":["pass_rate","wall_time","turns"],"success_condition":"Treatment pass_rate is higher while its deadline-miss rate is no higher; wall_time and turns quantify any efficiency shift."},"single_shot_ordinal":6}
